worksheet.title: Read and Change a Loop
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read & alter code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read a loop, change it, and say what happens.

parts.title: Read the code first
text: Good coders READ code before they change it — like reading a recipe before you cook.
Here is one of Bit's loops. Read it, see what it does, then change a number and predict the new result.

parts.title: Read this loop
parts.note: Bit moves 10 steps, 5 times. That is 5 moves and 50 steps in total.

parts.caption: Read it as 5 jumps of 10 → 50 steps.

parts.title: Read it
parts.prompt: Look at the loop above. How many times does Bit move? ______  Each move is 10 steps, so how far in TOTAL? ______

parts.title: Change the count, predict
parts.prompt: Change repeat 5 to repeat 3. PREDICT: how many moves now, and how far in total? Then check.

parts.title: Change the inside
parts.prompt: Now keep repeat 5, but change "move 10" to "move 2". How far does Bit go in total now? How did changing the inside block change the result?

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: You want Bit to move 40 steps in total, moving 10 each time. What repeat number do you need? Show how you worked it out.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Read a loop to see what it does. Changing the repeat number changes how many times; changing the inside block changes what happens each time.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students read a loop to say what it does, then change the repeat number or the inside block and describe how the result changes. There is also a work-backwards challenge. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the blocks and what Bit does, so you can teach from the printout. Optional: a Scratch-style app to drag the blocks and watch Bit run — you only press the green flag.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). Read the loop: 5 moves of 10 steps make 50 steps in total.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — 5 moves, 50 steps.
3. Let them work. Students change the repeat (Ex 2), change the inside block (Ex 3), and work backwards to a repeat number (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — 5 moves; 50 steps total. Exercise 2 — 3 moves; 30 steps.
Exercise 3 — 10 steps (5 × 2); changing the inside block changed how far each move goes. Exercise 4 (challenge) — repeat 4 (40 ÷ 10 = 4).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing the repeat when the question changes the inside block (or the other way around). Read which part changed.
Make it easier: write "moves × steps each" and fill in the numbers.
Make it harder: ask the repeat number for 60 steps at 10 each (6).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child reads the loop, changes one part, and works backwards to a repeat number.
